extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters, copyreaders, proofreaders, and editors
extracted.subtask_description: A newspaper stylebook covering punctuation, hyphenation, abbreviation and number conventions, proofreader marks, and newsroom terminology for producing and correcting newspaper copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractions (Use of apostrophe)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contractions. — Use an apostrophe in contracted words to indicate the omission of letters: as, couldn't, he'll, you're.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occasional exceptions to this general rule are found, where euphony would be violated by the additional s: as, Ulysses' son, Moses' staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation of compound words
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hyphen — Compound Words. — Put a hyphen between the members of a compound word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words compounded with these prefixes and suffixes are generally hyphenated: able-, brother-, by-, cross-, -elect, ex-, father-, great-, half-, -hand, mother-, open-, public-, quarter-, -rate, self-. In particular, hyphenate listed words (e.g., able-bodied, attorney-general, base-line, brother-in-law, life-saving, president-elect, to-day, to-night).

rubrics_metrics.name: Words written solid (closed compounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words Written Solid. — Words compounded of the following prefixes and suffixes are generally written solid: a-, after-, ante-, anti-, auto-, bi-, demi-, -ever, grand-, -holder, in-, inter-, intra-, -less, mid-, mis-, off-, on-, over-, post-, re-, -some, sub-, super-, tri-, un-, under-, up-, -ward, -wise, -with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The stylebook lists many specific closed compounds to be written solid (e.g., anyone, carload, baseball, football, landlady, typewriter, newcomer, postmaster, taxpayer, schoolboy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Words written separately (open compounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words Written Separately. — Write the following as two words: all right, any time, back yard, every time, ex officio, fellow man, half dollar, half dozen, half nelson, mass meeting, no one, pay roll, per cent, pro tem, some one, some way, squeeze play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists specific open compounds that should remain as two words rather than hyphenated or solid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation in compound numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound Numbers. — Compound numbers between twenty and a hundred, when spelled out, should have a hyphen: as, twenty-one, forty-three.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word division at line end (hyphenation and breaks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Word Division. — When dividing a word at the end of a line, observe specified rules to avoid incorrect or awkward splits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules enumerated: 1) Do not break a syllable (cre-ditable not cred-itable). 2) Do not divide a monosyllable (mob-bed not mo-bbed). 3) Do not separate a consonant from a vowel that affects its pronunciation (nec-essity not ne-cessity). 4) Do not divide a diphthong or separate successive vowels where one is silent (bowing not bo-wing). 5) Do not separate a syllable added by the addition of an s. 6) Do not divide hyphenated words except at the regular hyphen. 7) Do not make awkward divisions (nothing not noth-ing). 8) Do not begin a line with a hyphen. 9) As a rule, avoid dividing a word at the end of a line and never divide one at the end of a page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations — general avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviations Avoided. — Abbreviations should as a rule be avoided. The coming of the typewriter into journalism has created a tendency to write out all words in full.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations of personal and professional titles (before names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal and Professional Titles. — The following personal and professional titles are abbreviated when preceding proper names: Adjt. Gen., Brig. Gen., Capt., Col., Dr., Gen., Gov., Gov. Gen., Hon., Lieut., Lieut. Col., Lieut. Gen., Maj., Maj. Gen., Mr., Mrs., Miss?, Mme., Prof., Rev., Rt. Rev., Sergt., Supt., Mlle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List gives accepted abbreviated forms to use before names on newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of titles (rules for using Mr., Mrs., Miss, professional titles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of Titles. — Use personal titles under specified restrictions (numbered rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules include: 1) Do not use Mr. before a man's name when his baptismal name or initials are given. 2) After a person's name has been mentioned once, omit initials or Christian names thereafter and put a Mr. or professional title before the name. 3) If a person has more than one professional title, use the one of highest rank (or the one last received/commonly known). 4) Mrs. always precedes the name of a married woman; Miss that of an unmarried woman. 5) In lists of unmarried women, precede names with 'Misses' and give full Christian names. 6) In lists of married women, 'Mesdames' may introduce the names, though present usage prefers 'Mrs.' before each name. 7) When mentioning a man and his wife, use 'Mr. and Mrs. William Black' not 'William Black and wife.' 8) Do not use 'Master' before the name of a boy. 9) Before a 'Rev.' preceding the name always put 'the' (the Rev. T. P. Frost); if initials unknown, write 'the Rev. Mr. Frost' not 'the Rev. Frost.' Examples (Right/Wrong) are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of the months — abbreviations rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of the Months. — Abbreviations of the months, except March, April, May, June, and July, are permissible when followed by a numeral indicating the day of the month, but not when used alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Richard Malone ... Sept. 18' (right) vs. 'the middle of Sept.' (wrong).

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of the states — when to abbreviate
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of the States. — Names of states, territories, and island possessions of the United States are abbreviated when preceded by the name of a town or city: as, Pueblo, Col.; Manila, P. I.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miscellaneous acceptable abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Miscellaneous Abbreviations. — The following abbreviations are also in good usage: Esq., Inc., Jr., A.B., Ph.D., M.D., U.S.N., etc., when used after proper names; a.m., p.m., A.D., B.C., when preceded by numerals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbidden abbreviations (not used on most newspapers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forbidden Abbreviations. — Certain abbreviations may not be used on most newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categories given: 1) Christian names (e.g., Chas. for Charles, Thos. for Thomas). 2) Mount, Fort, and Saint (e.g., Mt. St. Elias for Mount Saint Elias). 3) Railroad, Company, Brothers, etc. (e.g., New Haven R. R. for New Haven Railroad, National Biscuit Co. for National Biscuit Company).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dates — how to write dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Dates. — Observe rules concerning dates: 1) Write year dates always in figures (e.g., 1776). 2) Write month dates in figures when preceded by the name of the month (e.g., July 7, 1916). When the name of the month does not precede, spell out the date (e.g., the tenth). 3) Do not write the day before the name of the month (avoid 'the 25th of December'). 4) Do not put a d, nd, st, or th after a date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided to show correct and incorrect forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Money — figures vs. words
rubrics_metrics.description: Money. — When mentioning sums of money, use figures for all amounts over one dollar; spell out all sums below a dollar: as, $5.75, fifty cents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If in the same sentence it becomes necessary to mention sums above and below a dollar, use figures for all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Street and district names with numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Street and District Names. — Spell out street, ward, district, and precinct names designated by numbers: as, Second ward, Tenth precinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sporting records — use of figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Sporting Records. — Use figures for sporting records: as, 10 feet, 5 inches; Time, 4:40; 18-2 balk-line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid beginning sentences with figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning of Sentences. — Do not begin a sentence with figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If impossible to shift the number to a later place in the sentence, place 'about' or 'more than' before the figures: 'More than 14,000 persons passed through the gates.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimensions — numeric notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Dimensions. — Use figures with an x to express dimensions of lots, buildings, floors, boats, machinery, etc.: as, 60x125 feet, 60-foot beam, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: General usage for numbers (when to use figures vs. spell out)
rubrics_metrics.description: General Usage. — Use figures to express dates, distances, latitude and longitude, hours of the day, degrees of temperature, percentage, street numbers, telephone numbers, automobile numbers, votes, and betting odds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In other cases spell out all numbers under 100, except where several numbers, some above and some under 100, are used in the same paragraph — in such a case, use figures for all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks used in correcting copy (editorial shorthand)
rubrics_metrics.description: MARKS USED IN CORRECTING COPY — A list of editorial shorthand abbreviations used by editors/proofreaders (amb = Ambiguous, and = A bad 'and' sentence, ant = Antecedent not clear, Cl = Not clear, Cst = Construction faulty, Coh = Coherence not good, Con = Wrong connective, Consult = Bring copy to instructor for discussion, 8 = Delete, dull = Dull reading, E = Error, ed = Editorializing, FW = 'Fine writing.', Gr = Bad grammar, K = Awkward, Id = Poor lead, P = Punctuation wrong, pt = Point of view shifted, qt = Make this a direct quotation, rep = Repetition, rew = Rewrite, sent = Use shorter sentences, SI = Slang, Sp = Bad spelling, SU = Sentence lacks unity, T = Wrong tense, unnec = Unnecessary details, tr = Transpose, W = Wrong use of word, ? = Truth of statement questioned, lf = Begin a new paragraph, No lf = No lf needed, J = Indent, O = Put the words together as one, # = Separate into two words, * = Hyphen needed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These marks constitute the standard shorthand for marking and correcting copy; examples and context appear in the list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-readers' marks (symbols and instructions)
rubrics_metrics.description: PROOF-READERS' MARKS — Symbols and standard proofreader instructions (Cap = Capitalize, lc = Lower case, 8 = Delete, stet = Restore crossed-out words, A = Insert at the place indicated, O = Insert a period, A (comma symbol) = Insert a comma, V = Insert quotation-marks, *l = Insert a hyphen, X = Imperfect letter, 9 = Letter inverted, lf = Make a new paragraph, No lf = No paragraph, # = Put a space between, ^-s = Smaller space, O (close up) = Close up; no space needed, V^ = Badly spaced; space more evenly, wf = Wrong font, tr = Transpose, [~~ = Carry to the left, Lower, Elevate, ^ = Straighten crooked line, lead = Add lead between the lines, 8 lead = Take out lead, (?) = Query: Is the proof correct?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard symbols used by proofreaders are defined with brief instructions for correcting proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology — newsroom glossary
rubrics_metrics.description: TERMINOLOGY — Definitions of common newsroom terms (Ad = Alley; Add. = Late news added; A. P. = Associated Press; Arrest Sheets; Assignment; Assignment Slips; Bank; Bank-man; Beat; B. F. = Bold-face; Blind Interview; Blotter; Box; Break-line; Bridge; Condensed Type; Copy; Copy Cutter; Copyholder; Copy-reader; Cover; Dead; Deck; Department Men; Display Type; Dope; etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive glossary entries define roles, processes, and production terms used in newspaper work (e.g., Galley Proof, Lead, Make-up, Morgue, Pull, Pyramid Head, Query, Release). This section serves as an operational vocabulary for reporters, editors, compositors, and proofreaders.
